title: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Learning Curves (March 2026)
author: Maxim Massenkoff · Eva Lyubich · Peter McCrory · Ruth Appel · Ryan Heller

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s distinction between AI usage, job transformation and demonstrated displacement. It materially extends the synthesis with evidence that experienced users achieve better outcomes through collaboration and that migration toward more automated API workflows may signal nearer-term work transformation, while not establishing unemployment effects or reduced junior hiring.
qs: More experienced users tend to use Claude more collaboratively, for more work-related reasons, in more complex tasks, and with more success.

As we note in our report on [labor market impacts](https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts), we expect that this migration from Claude.ai to the API may signal more imminent transformation of work for the associated jobs.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report reinforces the cluster’s account of uneven, capability-dependent augmentation and materially extends it with usage evidence that technically skilled early adopters achieve more successful interactions while facing greater disruption exposure. It also shows how migration to more directive API workflows may reduce human involvement, supporting the distinction between task reconfiguration and growing automation exposure. However, it is not legal-specific and does not directly assess verification or apprenticeship risks.
qs: Our analysis in this report identifies a channel through which such skill-biased transformation may already be unfolding: early adopters with high-skill tasks have more successful interactions with Claude than later, less technical adopters.
API workflows are far more likely to be directive, with less need for a human in the loop.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s selective-deployment and augmentation framing and materially extends it with large-scale observational evidence that experienced users collaborate more, undertake more complex work and achieve higher measured success. It also reinforces caution by treating learning-by-doing as plausible rather than causal and noting limited economic representativeness.
qs: More experienced users tend to use Claude more collaboratively, for more work-related reasons, in more complex tasks, and with more success.
While this could reflect sophistication of early adopters, it could also be evidence of learning-by-doing, where people get better at using Claude through experience.

st.t: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s distinction between observed platform use and realised workplace or employment effects. It shows that Claude usage is not economy-wide evidence and that experienced users tend toward iterative augmentation rather than greater delegation, while treating learning-by-doing and labour-market inequality as plausible rather than established causal outcomes.
qs: Overall, Claude is used for high-value, complex work that is not broadly representative of the US economy.

This pushes back against a hypothesis we made last year that automated use may be more typical of more experienced, sophisticated users; instead, we find that the most advanced users are more likely to iterate with Claude.

kp.k: Evidence covers Claude usage, not economy-wide adoption
kp.d: The report studies February 5–12, 2026 usage, three months after Claude Opus 4.5 and coincident with Opus 4.6's release, comparing it with November 2025 data. It samples 1 million conversations from both Claude.ai and the first-party API using privacy-preserving aggregated analysis; API data includes Claude Code but excludes third-party platforms. Its findings concern general AI usage rather than legal services specifically, and the authors explicitly caution that observed work is not broadly representative of the US economy.
qs: Our sample covers February 5 to February 12, three months following the release of Claude Opus 4.5 and coincident with the release of Claude Opus 4.6.
Overall, Claude is used for high-value, complex work that is not broadly representative of the US economy.

kp.k: Consumer usage diversified without substantially expanding observed task coverage
kp.d: Computer and Mathematical occupations still account for 35% of Claude.ai conversations, but the top 10 O*NET tasks fell from 24% in November 2025 to 19% in February 2026. Almost all observed tasks had appeared in earlier samples, and the cumulative estimate that 49% of jobs had at least a quarter of their tasks performed using Claude barely changed. The report notes that the occupational classification now uses 2019 O*NET-SOC codes rather than the previous 2010 vintage.
qs: Coding remains the most common use on our platforms, with tasks associated with Computer and Mathematical occupations accounting for 35% of conversations on Claude.ai
In our previous report, we noted that 49% of jobs had seen at least a quarter of their tasks performed using Claude.
Our data from this report showed many fewer novel O*NET tasks than in our previous report.

kp.k: Personal usage increased while coursework declined
kp.d: Between November 2025 and February 2026, coursework fell from 19% to 12% of Claude.ai conversations while personal use rose from 35% to 42%. The authors attribute part of the coursework decline to academic calendars: declines were 5 percentage points where school terms were active and 12 where most students were on break. Increasing signups brought more casual users; the sampling window also overlapped with Anthropic's Super Bowl advertisements.
qs: Coursework fell from 19% to 12% of conversations, while personal use rose from 35% to 42% of conversations.
The drop in coursework conversations was 5 percentage points in countries where the school term was active and 12 percentage points in the countries where most students were on break.

kp.k: Coding migrated toward agentic API workflows
kp.d: Since August 2025, the share of Computer and Mathematical tasks increased by 14% in the API and decreased by 18% in Claude.ai. Claude Code's architecture divides coding work into smaller API calls classified as distinct tasks, helping explain why API task concentration remained roughly flat between November and February despite growing coding activity. Over the longer August–February period, the top 10 API tasks increased from 28% to 33%. The authors interpret migration toward API workflows as a possible signal of more imminent occupational transformation, not demonstrated employment displacement.
qs: Claude Code’s agentic architecture splits coding work into smaller API calls, which are labeled as distinct tasks.
Since August 2025, the share of tasks in this category has increased by 14% in the API and decreased by 18% in Claude.ai.
Since August 2025, 1P API usage has become more concentrated, with the top 10 O*NET tasks now accounting for 33% of traffic, up from 28%.

kp.k: Collaboration increased despite API automation exposure
kp.d: Claude.ai augmentation increased slightly through validation and learning interactions; the body of the report states that automation decreased sharply in first-party API data. Nevertheless, API workflows remain much more likely to be directive and require less human involvement. The authors therefore distinguish changes in the observed interaction mix from the potential automation exposure associated with moving tasks into API workflows.
qs: Figure 1.3 shows that augmentation in Claude.ai increased slightly. This was driven by small bumps in validation and learning patterns.
API workflows are far more likely to be directive, with less need for a human in the loop.

kp.k: Sales and trading automation workflows expanded
kp.d: Business sales and outreach automation, and automated trading and market operations, each at least doubled their usage shares relative to three months earlier. Examples include lead qualification, customer-data enrichment, cold-email drafting, market monitoring and investment proposals. Identification required an O*NET task to appear at least 300 times in the current sample and exhibit at least 2x growth. These are workflow-usage findings; the report's suggestion that customer-service jobs may change as AI diffuses is a prospective interpretation of task exposure.
qs: We highlight two API workflows that appeared more frequently in February as compared to three months prior, with their shares at least doubling in our latest sample:
To find the emerging patterns, we filtered for O*NET tasks that (i) appeared at least 300 times in the current data and (ii) showed at least 2x growth compared to the previous report.

kp.k: Consumer task wage proxies and complexity declined slightly
kp.d: Estimated average task value on Claude.ai fell from $49.3 to $47.9, principally reflecting more simple factual questions and coding's migration to the API. Value is defined using associated occupations' average hourly wages, drawing on May 2024 BLS data, rather than measured productivity or realized economic gains. Human-input education requirements declined from 12.2 to 11.9 years, estimated human-only completion time fell about 2 minutes, and users granted greater autonomy. Conversely, tasks were judged slightly less possible for humans without AI. API task wage values rose over the report series.
qs: This estimate of the value of tasks in Claude.ai has dropped slightly from $49.3 to $47.9 mostly due to an increase in simple factual questions (e.g., sports outcomes, weather) and a decrease in coding as it shifts to the API.
Task value is estimated as the average hourly wage paid to workers who do that task.

The average years of education required for the human inputs declined from 12.2 to 11.9 years, users granted more autonomy to the AI, and the time required for the human to do the task alone fell by about 2 minutes.

kp.k: US adoption converged while international concentration increased
kp.d: The population-adjusted Anthropic Usage Index shows continued but slower convergence across US states. The top five states' share of per-person usage fell from 30% to 24% between August 2025 and February 2026; the top ten states' share fell from 40% to 38% since the previous report. Extrapolating current rates yields roughly equal per-capita state usage in 5–9 years rather than the earlier 2–5 years; this is a model-based projection. Internationally, the top 20 countries' share of population-adjusted usage increased from 45% to 48%, with rising inequality.
qs: From August 2025 to February 2026, the share of per-person usage going to the top five states has decreased from 30 to 24%.
we find that at this rate states would arrive at roughly equal usage per capita in 5–9 years, rather than 2–5.
The countries using Claude the most (per capita) now account for a larger share of overall usage, with the top 20 countries going from 45 to 48% of usage adjusted for population.

kp.k: Users select stronger models for higher-paid tasks
kp.d: Among paid Claude.ai accounts with access to all model classes, Opus handles 55% of Computer and Mathematical tasks versus 45% of Educational tasks, against 51% overall usage. In the occupation-level analysis, every additional $10 of task hourly wage is associated with a 1.5-percentage-point increase in Opus use on Claude.ai and 2.8 points in the API. The authors interpret these associations as broadly consistent with users matching capability, cost and usage limits to task demands, while offering technical familiarity and easier educational tasks as alternative explanations.
qs: for paid Claude.ai accounts, which have access to all model classes, 55% of Computer and Mathematical tasks (like coding software) use Opus, compared to 45% of Educational tasks.
Overall, for every additional $10 of hourly wage for a task, the share of conversations using Opus increases by 1.5 percentage points for Claude.ai users.
Its slope is about twice as large, with the Opus share increasing 2.8 percentage points for every $10 in task value.

kp.k: Experienced users collaborate more on complex work
kp.d: High tenure means signing up at least six months before the data pull. These users are more iterative and less directive, 7 percentage points more likely to use Claude for work, and undertake tasks with higher education requirements. Their top 10 tasks account for 20.7% of usage versus 22.2% among lower-tenure users. Across tenure, prompt education requirements rise almost one year per additional year since signup; personal conversations constitute 38% for users who signed up a year earlier versus 44% for newest users. These cross-sectional associations reverse the authors' earlier hypothesis that sophisticated users would automate more.
qs: High tenure users are more likely to use Claude to iterate on their work, and much less likely to delegate greater responsibility through directive use patterns.
They are 7 percentage points more likely to be using Claude for work, and use Claude for tasks that tend to require higher levels of education.

This pushes back against a hypothesis we made last year that automated use may be more typical of more experienced, sophisticated users; instead, we find that the most advanced users are more likely to iterate with Claude.

kp.k: Tenure predicts model-assessed success after statistical controls
kp.d: The report summarizes high-tenure users as having a 10% higher conversation success rate. Regression analysis reports an approximately 5-percentage-point unadjusted advantage, around 3 points with O*NET-task and request-cluster fixed effects, and 4 points with full controls. The authors also consider model selection, language, use case and country. Success is Claude's assessment of the conversation, not an independently verified work outcome. The remaining association is presented as consistent with improved ability to elicit useful responses, not causal proof of learning.
qs: Success is Claude’s assessment of whether the conversation was successful
The plot shows that long-tenure users are about 5 percentage points more likely to have a successful conversation.
This control moderates the effect somewhat, bringing it closer to 3 percentage points.
This regression yields a slightly higher impact of high tenure, suggesting a 4-percentage-point higher success rate accounting for the full controls.

kp.k: Learning-by-doing remains confounded by selection and survivorship
kp.d: The authors explicitly retain cohort characteristics and survivorship as alternative explanations: early adopters may be more technical, and continuing users may have tasks especially suited to Claude. Users who signed up previously but stopped using it are unobserved. Narrow within-task comparisons rule out simple task-composition explanations but do not fully isolate learning-by-doing. The authors state that cleaner separation of these mechanisms will require further observation over time.
qs: The high-tenure users are self-selected and the differences here could reflect stable characteristics.
We do not observe people who signed up a year ago but are no longer using Claude.
Over time, we will be able to more cleanly isolate cohort and survivorship bias from learning-by-doing.

kp.k: Unequal learning opportunities may reinforce labor-market inequality
kp.d: The report proposes a skill-biased technological-change mechanism: early adopters undertaking high-skill tasks have more successful interactions, potentially allowing unequal adoption and complementary expertise to produce self-reinforcing benefits. It suggests that these workers may be both particularly exposed to disruption and particularly aided during initial augmentative adoption. These are possible labor-market implications of observed usage and success differences, not measured wage effects or demonstrated displacement.
qs: These observed differences in success rates could deepen inequalities in the labor market.

Our analysis in this report identifies a channel through which such skill-biased transformation may already be unfolding: early adopters with high-skill tasks have more successful interactions with Claude than later, less technical adopters.

These early-adopting users may simultaneously be the [most exposed](https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts) to AI-driven disruption and most aided by AI in these initial, augmentative waves of adoption.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Anthropic’s report authors claim that experience is associated with more successful, collaborative AI use; adoption is diversifying; and migration into API workflows may signal greater automation exposure. These are cross-domain claims, not findings about legal services.
pts.d: Massenkoff, Lyubich, McCrory, Appel and Heller report that users with at least six months’ tenure undertake more complex, work-related tasks, collaborate more, and achieve higher conversation success rates. They interpret this as consistent with learning-by-doing, while retaining cohort effects and survivorship bias as alternatives. This reverses their earlier hypothesis that experienced users would favor automated use. Users also select Opus more frequently for higher-wage tasks, with a stronger relationship in API traffic. Claude.ai usage diversified between November 2025 and February 2026: the top ten tasks fell from 24% to 19% of conversations, personal use rose, and the occupational-wage proxy for average task value declined from $49.3 to $47.9. Coding migrated toward more automated API workflows, which the authors suggest may herald more imminent work transformation. Sales/outreach and trading/market-operations workflows each at least doubled their sampled shares. The authors further suggest that experienced early adopters’ greater success could reinforce labor-market inequality. They do not establish actual wage changes or job displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of Anthropic’s observational Claude usage data, task classifications, occupational-wage proxies, and controlled regressions—not direct measurements of employment effects or independently verified task outcomes.
pts.d: The authors describe sampling one million conversations from both Claude.ai and the first-party API, including Claude Code, using privacy-preserving aggregate analysis. They compare usage with earlier Economic Index samples and map tasks to O*NET occupations. Task value is a proxy based on May 2024 US BLS occupational wages, rather than measured economic output or revenue. Conversation success is assessed by Claude. High-tenure users’ success advantage is about five percentage points in a bivariate regression, about three points after task and request-cluster fixed effects, and about four points with fuller controls; the summary describes a 10% higher success rate. These are different presentations of the association, not evidence that experience causally produces a ten-percentage-point gain. Emerging API workflows were identified by requiring at least 300 current-sample appearances and at least twofold growth. The authors acknowledge that early-adopter selection and continued-user survivorship could explain some results. The inequality and occupational-transformation claims are interpretations of observed usage, not demonstrated labor-market outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Findings concern February 5–12, 2026 usage, principally compared with November 2025; predictions about work transformation and inequality are conditional and largely undated.
pts.d: Published March 24, 2026, the report samples usage three months after Opus 4.5’s release and during Opus 4.6’s release. Some platform and geographic comparisons begin in August 2025. High tenure means signup at least six months before the data pull, not a measured amount of active practice. Learning-by-doing remains a possible explanation rather than an isolated causal effect. Changes in usage mix may partly reflect academic calendars and an influx of first-time users during Anthropic’s Super Bowl advertisements. API task counts are also shaped by Claude Code’s architecture, which divides coding work into smaller calls. The geographic projection is explicitly conditional on the observed convergence rate: roughly equal US state usage per capita in five to nine years, revised from two to five years, with the range reflecting weighted versus unweighted estimates. No corresponding timetable is given for occupational automation or inequality effects.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are Claude users and AI-exposed occupations across the economy, with different implications for experienced technical users, newer casual users, API adopters, and lower-adoption regions.
pts.d: Experienced and often technical early adopters obtain more successful interactions and may enjoy reinforcing advantages, while also facing AI disruption exposure. Newer users more often bring simpler personal tasks. Coding workers and customer-service representatives are highlighted as potentially facing work transformation as tasks enter automated API workflows; sales/outreach and trading/market-operations activities are additional emerging examples. Model-choice differences concern both consumer-facing users and developers deploying programmatic workflows. Geographically, usage remains concentrated in high-income countries and US knowledge-worker locations. US state usage is converging, whereas low-adoption countries fell further behind in relative terms. The cumulative observation that about 49% of jobs have had at least a quarter of their tasks represented in Claude usage is a task-coverage measure, not the proportion of workers displaced. The report does not identify law firms, lawyers, legal departments, or legal-service clients as separately affected groups.
